idiom_name: JavaFX Property wrappers (SimpleStringProperty) + ChangeListener/Bindings + FXML controllers
implementation_notes: JavaFX turns every bean property into an observable: the view-model exposes StringProperty / DoubleProperty members with the conventional getter, setter and property accessor, views in FXML bind with ${...} expressions or register listeners, and the Bindings/fluent API derives values so dependent controls update automatically. The property implementations evaluate lazily, so invalidation and change events differ: a ChangeListener forces eager computation, while an InvalidationListener only tells you the value is no longer valid. Use the property accessor for binding and keep the plain getter for ordinary consumers.
pitfalls: Binding with bind() makes the target read-only: writing to a bound property throws - use bindBidirectional() for editors.
Registering a ChangeListener enforces eager computation of a lazily evaluated binding; use an InvalidationListener when you only need to know that something changed.
Holding property objects in long-lived view-models keeps registered listeners (and their views) alive unless listeners are removed on teardown.
Properties must be touched on the JavaFX application thread; updates from background tasks need Platform.runLater.

variants.name: Android ViewModel + LiveData observed from Activities/Fragments (Java)
variants.idiom_name: androidx ViewModel + MutableLiveData with lifecycle-aware observers (Java)
variants.implementation_notes: On Android the ViewModel survives configuration changes and exposes MutableLiveData (or immutable LiveData) that the view observes with observe(lifecycleOwner, observer); LiveData is lifecycle-aware, so inactive observers are not notified and are dropped at DESTROYED, which removes the manual unbinding that makes classic MVVM leak-prone. Java screens obtain the view-model through ViewModelProvider and update state with setValue/postValue. Reach for this route on Java-only legacy screens; Kotlin with Compose/StateFlow is the current default elsewhere.
pitfalls: setValue must be called on the main thread (postValue from background): mixing them up either crashes or reorders updates.
A ViewModel must never hold an Activity, View or Context reference - it outlives the screen and leaks it (use AndroidViewModel or injected application context).
LiveData is not a stream: transformations are synchronous and there is no reduce/replay for composite state, so multi-field screens drift into many separate LiveData fields.
onChanged is called with the last value when an observer becomes active again: observer code must be idempotent and must not re-trigger writes.
